paper_title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

sections.content: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce INTO THE UNKNOWN, benchmark that provides an agent with science paper along with research direction to pursue and tasks it to write follow-up paper. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Given research direction from scientist, can an AI agent autonomously carry out the experiments and write them up as scientific paper? The recent advancement of AI agents capable of solving long-horizon tasks makes pursuing this question more timely [13]. Scientific research is open-ended, however, which makes it difficult to benchmark: for research question no one has yet answered, there is no reference answer to directly compare and grade solution against [4, 5]. Some prior works use AI reviewers to grade AI-written papers [6, 7], but AI reviewers are known to have their own limitations [8, 9], making such assessments unreliable. To address this, we introduce INTO THE UNKNOWN, benchmark that gives an AI agent scientific paper, tasks it to write follow-up, and assesses the outcome against scientist-verified rubrics. As shown in Figure 1, our key idea is that the space of possible research can be constrained to set of follow-up directions defined by human experts, which makes reliable evaluation possible. Specifically, the scientist proposes concrete research direction and specifies the necessary conditions that follow-up paper must satisfy. INTO THE UNKNOWN hence evaluates the full research process that runs from an idea to completed paper by checking whether the resulting paper satisfies these conditions. This extends the scope of prior benchmarks, which simulate parts of the research process via tasks with stated target, such as reproducing published paper [10, 11] or executing computational workflow [12]. To construct the INTO THE UNKNOWN, we work with domain scientists currently or formerly affiliated with US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories. Each scientist recommends their papers which are published or near published at prestigious venues, and whose experiments are computational, so that follow-up can be carried 1 Figure 1: Specifying the follow-up direction and formulating the scientists bar as rubrics make evaluation of open-ended research tractable. (a) For an explicit implementation of the LCHS quantum algorithm [13], its first author states the direction and the bar. (b) The space of possible follow-ups S1 is unbounded; fixing the direction narrows it to S2, and the scientists bar narrows it further to S3. (c) Each clause of the bar becomes an item in the direction-specific rubric (yellow) or the integrity rubric (blue). Evaluation checks whether submission falls in S3. out in code alone. Then, they propose follow-up direction from each paper that remains unpublished and that, if carried out well, would merit publication in their standards. We iterate with them until the direction and the necessary conditions follow-up paper must satisfy are documented as task specification and rubric. In total, we collect 15 open research problems from 10 scientists across domains including quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The necessary conditions each scientist specifies are documented as two rubrics: direction-specific rubric formalizing what successful follow-up must establish, and an integrity rubric formalizing what would make submission untrustworthy regardless of what it reports, such as results in the paper that do not trace to the logs that produced them. Using these, we assess submission along three conditions: (C1) Integrity, whether the work is free of fabrication or unverifiable claims (i.e., it satisfies all conditions from the integrity rubric); (C2) Completeness, whether the paper and code are complete enough to be graded (i.e., it satisfies the conditions from the direction-specific rubric related to the required deliverables); and (C3) Sufficiency, whether the work clears the bar the scientist set (i.e., it satisfies the success conditions specified in the direction-specific rubric). Such assessment replaces subjective and hard-to-answer question, whether paper is doing good science, with tractable one: whether the work is honest, complete, and meets standard the domain scientist set. Across 135 submissions from nine frontier agents, which took 1,942.81 hours to generate and 62.95 hours to evaluate in wall-clock time, none clears all three conditions. Most fail the integrity check: 114 of the 135 submissions are not honest, most often through claims of work that was never done, mismatches between the paper, its code, and its protocol, or numerical claims that contradict the recorded evidence, and only three agents pass C1 on any submission (GPT-6-Astra on 11 of 15, GPT-5.6-Sol on 6, and Claude-Opus-5.5 on 4). Inspecting the trajectories, we find recurring weaknesses that help explain these failures, including lenient self-verification, insufficient backtracking, and self-directed scope reduction. Overall, agents readily produce work that looks like follow-up paper, but none passes the bar set by the scientist. Based on these results, we position INTO THE UNKNOWN as challenging testbed for training better agents and developing harnesses for scientific research. 2 Figure 2: Task formulation of INTO THE UNKNOWN. The AI agent is given task specification, the original paper, along with its code and data. The AI agent should instantiate the scientists idea (in the task specification) by submitting follow-up paper and also provide the code and logs.

sections.title: 2.2 Construction process
sections.content: Paper selection. The 15 science papers span quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning, and were selected for their relevance to research conducted at United States Department of Energy national laboratories.1 We apply three selection criteria for choosing these papers: (1) whether scientist among the papers first or last authors can be recruited to take part in constructing the benchmark; (2) whether the papers experiments are computational, so that follow-up can be carried out in code alone; and, (3) for papers published in 2024 or earlier, whether the work is well cited within its field. 1One of the 15 papers is an exception and has no national laboratory scientist among its authors; it was included to cover topic (physics-informed neural networks) not represented in the rest of the set. 4 As shown in Table 1, the set is split into two groups: 8 papers published in journal or conference in 2024 or earlier (denoted as Group A), and 7 papers submitted in 2026 that are not yet published or were accepted recently (denoted as Group B). Note that citation count is not meaningful signal for the Group papers, so we rely on the involved scientists judgment that the work is worth building on. This split is deliberate: the two groups let us ask if an agent can write follow-up regardless of whether the original work is established (Group A) or new (Group B). It is notable that these directions cover more than optimize tasks (i.e., proposing method that outperforms baseline on pre-defined metric). Some do take this form, such as reducing the number of stochastic probes that Projected Hessian Learning requires (P11) or reconstructing functions faster than existing acquisition strategies (P4). About half, however, are exploratory: stress-testing where method breaks down (P6, P13), testing scientific hypothesis (P7, P14), or determining how much hardware noise an algorithm can tolerate (P10). For these, the agent must decide what experiment would answer the question before running it, and there is no single metric to optimize. Curating the task specifications and rubrics & expert verification. At the initial round, we ask scientists two questions: (1) propose follow-up direction for their own paper that, to the best of their knowledge, remains unpublished but would have the potential to be published if executed well; (2) verbalize the criteria they would require submission to meet for the direction to count as having been pursued successfully. Upon receiving the responses, we use an AI agent (Claude-Opus-5 max effort with claude-code-cli as the harness) to draft an initial version of the , Rdirection, and Rintegrity. Subsequently, we format these as file in which the domain scientists can review and edit. In total, 112 edits were made by domain scientists and they are listed in Appendix C. Preparing the workspaces of agents. Instantiating the given follow-up direction for each of the 15 papers requires working from the data and code named in the task specification. Human scientists likewise often build on the artifacts of prior work directly, editing them as needed, not constructing everything from scratch. To reflect this, we download the necessary code repositories and datasets in advance and place them under code/ and data/ in the workspace before launching the agent session. This also isolates the agents ability to pursue new direction from its ability to reimplement existing work. Furthermore, because supplying the original paper as PDF can hinder comprehension, we convert it to Markdown beforehand with Mistral OCR [30].

sections.title: 3 Experimental setup
sections.content: Baselines. We evaluate nine AI agents (both open-weight and proprietary agents) considered frontier as of August 2026: Claude-Opus-4.8, Claude-Opus-5, Claude-Fable-5, GPT-5.6-Sol, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 [31], Kimi-K3 [32], and GLM-5.3 [33]. Each model runs within its native agentic harness: claude-agent-sdk, codex-sdk, deepseekharness, and kimi-agent-sdk, respectively. GLM-5.3 has no publicly released native agentic sdk harness, so we run it with software-agent-sdk [34]. All models run at their max context length (1 million) and max reasoning efforts. Automated Judges. We use GPT-6-Astra with codex-sdk as the harness, max reasoning effort, and maximum context length as the automated agentic judge [15]. We report average@4, at the node-level. We provide analysis of the reliability and consistency of the automated judge at Appendix and Appendix B. Compute and time budget for agents. To provide each agent with adequate resources, we consult the domain scientist for each paper. Six papers that require GPU resources2 receive one node of 8H200, and the other nine papers receive 1Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C (Ice Lake) @ 2.9 GHz, with 32 vCPUs (16 physical cores 2 threads), 54 MiB L3 cache, and 61 GiB of usable RAM (64 GiB nominal), and 1 TB of storage is provided. Given the difficulty of the task, we impose no time limit and let it continue until the agent terminates its own session. Ralph Wiggum loop. The Ralph Wiggum loop is method of iteratively relaunching an agent to review and improve its submission, and is frequently used for software engineering tasks [35]. In early experiments, we find that agents often terminate the session without complete submission. We therefore allow up to five rounds of the loop so that model can continue working in the same workspace. Whenever an agent ends its session, we relaunch it and have it assess the state of its workspace. If it judges that its own submission is complete, we stop relaunching. Internet access. Seeking additional information online (e.g., searching the literature, referencing technical documentations) is essential to conduct research. Because our follow-up directions are verified by the original authors as having no known published counterpart, we do not restrict internet access, unlike agent benchmarks that prohibits it [36, 37]. Agents may therefore use curl or the built-in search tools of each harness to access the internet, in addition to the context provided by default (the original paper, its data, and its code). 2The six papers are P1 [16], P2 [17], P8 [23], P9 [13], P11 [25], P13 [27]. 5 Table 2: Results on the INTO THE UNKNOWN benchmark. sections.title: 4 Experimental results
sections.content: Table 2 reports the main results for all 135 submissions (nine agents on 15 papers). Notably, no agent produces valid submission under our grading (i.e., strict grading for G1 G2 G3). Most submissions fail the integrity checks (G1). On the strict G1 column of Table 2, only three agents have any submission that passes all the nodes of Rintegrity: GPT-6-Astra on 11 of its 15 papers (73.33%), GPT-5.6-Sol on 6 (40.00%), and Claude-Opus-5.5 on 4 (26.67%). Every submission from the other six agents fails at least one of the nodes. Almost grading, which passes gate when at least 90% of its nodes pass, raises these three agents to 86.67%, 60.00%, and 60.00%, but leaves the other six at 0.00%. As shown in the left panel of Figure 3, we group the recorded violations of the 114 failing submissions into seven non-exclusive categories. The most frequent are mismatch between the paper and its code (90 submissions), reported numbers that contradict the evidence (85 submissions), and false claims of completed work (68 submissions). Some failures concentrate in open-weight agents, where out of the 15 submissions that misreport baseline results, 12 come from DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3, and two submissions that includes hard-coded results come from Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. 6 Almost no submission is complete (G2). On the strict G2 column of Table 2, only one of the 135 submissions is complete, from GPT-6-Astra; it also passes G1, making it the only honest and complete submission. Under almost grading, GPT-6-Astra completes 53.33% of its submissions and Claude-Opus-5.5 26.67%, while no other agent exceeds 6.67%. The right panel of Figure 3 shows that this failure is nearly universal. 128 of the 135 submissions provide inadequate required files or records, the artifacts the task specification requires alongside the paper, such as timestamped plan file written before the evaluation runs, per-seed training logs, or record of attempted work. No submission meets the domain scientists bar (G3). Every agent scores 0.00% on the strict G3 column, and therefore 0.00% on our main metric (G1 G2 G3. Almost grading shows that few submissions come close: GPT-6-Astra reaches 26.67%, Claude-Opus-5.5 and GPT-5.6-Sol 20.00%, and Claude-Fable-5 13.33%, while the other five agents remain at 0.00%. As shown in the right panel of Figure 3, every one of the 135 submissions fails the direction-specific rubric. Beyond missing deliverables, the most frequent failures are unmet method or protocol requirements (120 submissions) and inadequate analysis or explanation (104 submissions), while 83 submissions miss the scientific targets the scientist specified. Open-weight agents fail the literature and originality requirements more often, on 34 of their 45 submissions compared with 29 of the 90 from proprietary agents. Node-level grading still separates agents. Although strict paper-level scores are almost all zero, node-level pass rates distinguish the performance among agents. GPT-6-Astra passes the most nodes on both rubrics (97.77% of integrity nodes and 83.62% of direction-specific nodes), followed by Claude-Opus-5.5 (90.38% and 80.00%) and GPT-5.6-Sol (88.73% and 74.89%). The open-weight agents pass the fewest direction-specific nodes, between 44.25% and 52.86%, while their integrity pass rates overlap with those of Claude-Opus-4.8, Claude-Opus-5, and Claude-Fable-5. Agents differ in how close they come to the scientists bar, even though there is no valid submission.

sections.title: 5.1 Behaviors that inhibit AI agents from conducting scientific research
sections.content: The results in section 4 raise the question of why every submission remains incomplete or falls short of the scientists bar, even though agents (1) receive detailed task specifications, (2) have no imposed time limit and access to substantial compute, and (3) can retry up to five times (i.e., the Ralph Wiggum loop). To answer this, we randomly sample 64 of the 105 submissions, spanning all nine evaluated agents, and manually inspect their trajectories. We identify three recurring behaviors: Lenient self-verification: Agents treat limited checks as evidence that broader task requirements are satisfied, or accept results as satisfactory despite contradictory evidence. Hence, agents are not strict enough when checking its own work and whether task is complete. Insufficient backtracking: Agents recognize an unmet requirement but instead of trying to fix it, choose to document the shortfall or proceed with suboptimal solution. The issue is not negative scientific finding itself, but the decision to stop pursuing specified objective. Self-directed scope reduction: Agents replace required work with fewer experiments, an easier comparison, or narrower objective without authorization. Such changes can be reasonable in research, but means agents cant autonomously carry out specified direction. As shown in Figure 4, we observe lenient self-verification in 58 of the 64 submissions, insufficient backtracking in 34, and selfdirected scope reduction in 21. Prior literature identifies verification and backtracking as behaviors that support self-improvement in reasoning models [38]. Our findings suggest that reliably applying these behaviors across long-horizon scientific research remains challenging. Future work could investigate harness designs and post-training methods that encourage stricter verification, sustained backtracking, and adherence to task requirements. We provide trajectory excerpts and audit notes in Appendix D. In Figure 5, we present two examples: one illustrating lenient selfverification, and the other illustrating insufficient backtracking. Figure 4: Behaviors from 64 audited trajectories. Categories are non-exclusive, since one trajectory can exhibit several behaviors. 7 Figure 5: Two examples of verification and backtracking failures. (Left) Claude-Fable-5 derives its completion checker from an incomplete experiment schedule, so the checker reports all scheduled runs as complete while four runs are missing. (Right) GPT-5.6-Sol acknowledges unmet scientific objectives and proceeds to write the paper; its subsequent coverage check does not establish success. As shown in Figure 5 (left), Claude-Fable-5 plans to evaluate four kernel families at both nk = 6 and nk = 7, but its experiment launcher includes these families only at nk = 7. It then builds completion checker that reuses the launchers configuration list instead of independently checking coverage against the original plan. Consequently, the checker reports 41/41 completed runs and no missing outputs, even though the four planned nk = 6 experiments are never scheduled. Overall, this illustrates how lenient self-verification at one step can persist throughout long-horizon research task: the agent continues to trust its checker during later reviews without verifying that it covers the original plan, leaving required experiments missing. As shown in Figure 5 (right), GPT-5.6-Sol observes that its method outperforms the baseline on an 80/20 split but underperforms it when fitted to the full dataset. Later, after substantial attempts to improve the method, it explicitly acknowledges that the method also misses the strict sample-efficiency target and performs worse on all three transfer materials. Instead of resuming method development, it proceeds to write the paper around these outcomes and checks that the experimental records are complete. This illustrates how insufficient backtracking can leave recognized scientific shortfalls unresolved: rather than revising its method or starting over with an alternative approach, the agent proceeds to report its limitations while objectives remain unmet.

sections.title: 5.2 Does longer execution time correspond to better outcomes?
sections.content: Experimental setup. We measure the elapsed execution time and the number of recorded steps for all 135 submissions from nine agents on 15 papers, and visualize both by agent in Figure 6. Since almost no submission 8 Table 3: Association between recorded effort and rubric pass rates. Pass rates are the fractions of rubric nodes passed. Comparisons pair different agents on the same paper (within paper) or different papers attempted by the same agent (within agent). We report mean Somers with pointwise 95% confidence intervals and approximate p-values from 20,000 paper-level bootstrap resamples; padj is the p-value after Holm correction across all comparisons, and bold marks padj < 0.05. Negative indicates lower pass rates with greater effort. Note that harnesses record steps at different granularities, so within-paper step comparisons are descriptive, and should be taken with grain of salt. Longer runs do not correspond to better submissions. Comparing the effort in Figure 6 with the pass rates in Table 2, the agents that run longest do not produce the strongest submissions. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 has the longest median execution time at 19.5 hours, followed by GLM-5.3 at 13.9 hours, yet these two agents pass among the fewest direction-specific rubric nodes (52.55% and 45.09%). GPT-5.6-Sol has the shortest median at 2.9 hours, but passes the most nodes on both rubrics and is the only agent with submissions that pass the integrity checks. Step counts show similar pattern: Kimi-K3 records the most steps, with median of 4,409, while passing only 59.16% of integrity nodes and 54.13% of direction-specific nodes. The two measures also diverge across agents, since DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 runs the longest while recording the fewest steps (median 261), which reflects in part how differently each harness counts steps. Because these comparisons pair different agents, they largely reflect differences between agents, as the slowest agents are also among the weakest. Within the same agent, neither execution time nor step count shows meaningful association with either pass rate, with estimates close to zero and confidence intervals spanning zero. Taken together, we find no evidence that running longer yields better submissions, either across agents or for given agent. These are observational comparisons across 15 papers and nine agents, and we suspect future agents to use additional execution time more effectively to produce higher-quality papers.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: AI agents for scientific research. Agents for scientific research have expanded from individual stages of the research process toward the process as whole [4042]. Earlier systems target single stage, such as generating research ideas [43], searching and synthesizing the literature [44, 45], or writing code for stated analysis [46]. More recent systems chain these stages into end-to-end pipelines that propose an idea, implement it, run experiments, and write the result as paper [6, 7, 47]. In these pipelines the agent chooses its own research question, so weak paper may reflect poor idea, poor execution, or both. INTO THE UNKNOWN instead supplies the direction from the author of the original paper, so we evaluate whether an agent can carry out direction scientist would pursue. Benchmarks for research agents. Benchmarks for these agents make evaluation tractable by grading submission against an anchor, and in each case the anchor exists because human has already done the work. Some anchor on published result: PaperBench asks an agent to replicate an ICML paper from scratch and grades it against rubric co-developed with the papers authors [11]. Others anchor on recorded human performance, scoring submissions against Kaggle medal thresholds [48], published state-of-the-art values [49], or expert attempts on the same environments [50]. third group anchors on reference solution written for evaluation. Terminal-BenchScience is closest to ours in who sets the bar, since its tasks are contributed by practicing scientists [12], but each task is workflow the contributing scientist has already run, which is why it ships with an oracle solution and programmatic tests. FrontierScience likewise grades expert-authored items against reference solution or an expert rubric [51]. In contrast, the follow-up directions in INTO THE UNKNOWN have not yet been pursued by anyone. Evaluating research without an anchor. Without an anchor, evaluation has to judge the research output directly. common approach is an AI reviewer, used both within end-to-end pipelines [6, 7] and in MLR-Bench, where the agent proposes its own idea, submits full paper, and is scored by LLM reviewers on dimensions such as clarity, novelty, and soundness [52]. AI reviewers, however, have known limitations [8, 9], and paper can read as sound while resting on experiments that were never run as described: Chen et al. [52] report fabricated or invalidated results in roughly 80% of their coding-agent tasks, and Si et al. [43] find that the apparent novelty of LLM-generated ideas largely disappears once they are executed. Human experts are more reliable but do not scale, and Kirgis et al. [53] have the authors of two unpublished papers grade agent attempts only after the submissions exist. INTO THE UNKNOWN grades against criteria the author specifies, formalized as leaf-level questions.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We present INTO THE UNKNOWN, benchmark that tasks AI agents to write follow-up papers of 15 scientific papers from US DOE national laboratories, where the follow-up directions are proposed by the original paper authors. We find that current frontier AI agents are not yet capable of executing the research ideas provided by domain scientists, and that the resulting submissions are unreliable, incomplete, and fail to meet the standard of scientists. Our analyses show that the reasons agent fail are due to lenient verification, insufficient backtracking, and self-directed scope reduction. Furthermore, we find that longer execution time doesnt necessarily correlate to higher-quality submission. Looking ahead, we envision INTO THE UNKNOWN as testbed for developing scientific research agents, via better agentic post-training methods and specialized harnesses.

Automated grading with LLM-as-a-Judge [5456] or Agent-as-a-Judge [15] makes assessment convenient, but it is known to suffer from various biases [57, 58] and often fails to match the granularity of expert judgment [5961]. To test whether our grading pipeline provides reliable estimate of the quality of AI-written papers, we conduct meta-verification study that collects expert judgments on these papers and compares them with the judgments of our pipeline. Expert validation study setup. For each original paper, we provide its author with an annotation sheet and three AI-generated follow-up papers, produced by Claude-Opus-5, Claude-Fable-5, and GPT-5.6-Sol. The papers are anonymized and presented in random order, so the expert does not know which agent produced which paper. We ask the expert to answer three questions for each paper: Q1. Meeting the follow-up direction: Given the follow-up direction, did this submission succeed in meeting the goal? Q2. Major reviewer weaknesses: If you were reviewing this paper for journal or conference, what would you point out as its major weaknesses? Q3. Scientific quality and impact: Compared to your original paper, is this AI-generated paper anywhere near the same standard of scientific quality or impact? Q1 asks what the rubrics are designed to measure, which lets us test whether rubrics constructed before the scientists saw any AI-generated paper reproduce the judgments they make after reading one. Q2 and Q3 ask about aspects the rubrics were not explicitly designed to target, and we include them for two reasons. First, they reveal what scientist requires beyond the necessary conditions encoded in the rubrics, that is, what separates submission that clears the bar from one the scientist would consider good science. Second, the weaknesses scientists raise after reading submission can be turned into additional rubric items (i.e., rubric evolution [62]), so the rubrics can be refined as agents improve and new failures appear. Meta-verification setup. Following the meta-verification protocol of Kim et al. [9], we manually split the responses to Q1, Q2, and Q3 into individual criticisms. Treating these criticisms as the gold standard, we measure the reliability of our pipeline in two ways. Rubric coverage is the fraction of expert criticisms addressed by at least one rubric item, and matching assessments is the fraction of covered criticisms on which the pipelines verdict agrees with the experts. We report (1) each metric averaged per paper (each papers percentage as one data point), and (2) pooled across all criticisms. A.2 Experimental results The results are shown in Table 4. The rubrics reproduce expert judgments on what they are designed to measure. For Q1, the rubrics cover all 41 expert judgments on whether submission met its follow-up direction, and the pipelines verdict agrees with the experts on every one. Rubrics constructed before the scientists saw any AI-generated paper therefore reproduce the judgments the scientists make after reading one. 15 Table 5: Consistency across four repeated judgments. Both judges evaluate the same 52 submissions. Percentages measure agreement across all four runs on the overall submission grade, each cumulative pass decision, or the exact node rating. Unresolved and not-applicable node ratings remain distinct categories. Both judges use the current grading policy. Brackets show 95% confidence intervals from 20,000 whole-paper bootstrap resamples; [100, 100] reflects no variation in the observed sample, not guaranteed agreement on new submissions. Consistency measurement (%) Codex judge (GPT-6-Astra) Claude-code judge (Claude-Opus-5.5) Same overall grade 86.5% [78.8, 94.1] 57.7% [47.1, 68.0] Judgment on passing G1 Judgment on passing G1 G2 Judgment on passing G1 G2 G3 86.5% [78.8, 94.1] 100.0% [100.0, 100.0] 100.0% [100.0, 100.0] Direction-specific rubric node rating Integrity-check rubric node rating 89.7% [88.4, 91.0] 87.6% [85.3, 89.7] 69.2% [57.7, 80.8] 78.8% [68.6, 88.5] 98.1% [93.9, 100.0] 94.9% [93.9, 95.8] 92.7% [90.4, 94.6] The rubrics anticipate most weaknesses reviewer would raise. For Q2, the rubrics cover 96.97% of the major weaknesses experts identify when reading as reviewers (93.98% pooled), and the pipeline agrees with the expert on 80.34% of those (83.20% pooled). Although the rubrics were not built to anticipate reviewer criticisms, they address nearly all of them, suggesting that the necessary conditions scientists specify in advance capture most of what they find lacking after reading the paper. Scientific quality and impact remain partly beyond the rubrics. For Q3, coverage falls to 89.05% (75.34% pooled) and agreement to 68.68% (63.64% pooled), with wide confidence intervals. This is expected, since judgments of quality and impact go beyond the necessary conditions the rubrics encode. The lower pooled coverage further indicates that uncovered criticisms concentrate in papers on which experts raised more points, so the rubrics miss the most where experts have the most to say. Takeaway. Overall, coverage and agreement decrease steadily from Q1 to Q3, tracking the distance from what the rubrics are designed to measure. This supports using the rubrics as reliable check on the necessary conditions scientist sets, while judgments of scientific merit require expert verification. Towards measuring scientific merit. The Q3 criticisms that the rubrics miss or misjudge are mostly criticisms that require subjective evaluation, which is crucial but hard-to-verify. For instance, one expert wrote The paper do not tell story. They do not take the readers hand and walk them through the findings, judgment about narrative that no rubric item could well model. subtler case arises for the follow-up to P2, where the expert noted that prior work statements are made as summaries of that work and not how it motivated the present work. Two rubric items address this concern, asking whether the methods motivation is grounded in published literature and how substantively the paper engages with it. The judge rates both as substantive with high confidence, noting that the papers Introduction, Design Rationale, and Related Work compare SLIM with SNAP, SOAP/GAP, MTP, ACE, DeePMD. . . The expert does not dispute that these comparisons exist; they dispute whether the comparisons explain why the method takes its particular form, and the judges explanation identifies no such connection. Telling apart paper that cites prior work from one that builds on it requires judging the quality of an argument, which is subjective and noisy for an automated judge. We therefore do not intend the rubrics to measure it, instead, they check the necessary conditions scientist sets, and judgments of this kind remain the role of expert review.

sections.title: B Consistency of Automated Grading
sections.content: B.1 Experimental setup Motivation. Beyond agreeing with expert judgments, an automated grading pipeline should also be consistent: grading the same submission again should yield the same verdict. LLM judges sample their outputs, so repeated runs on the same submission can disagree, which threatens the reproducibility of benchmark scores. This concern is sharper for our pipeline, since each paper-level decision requires every relevant node to pass, and single node rated differently across runs can change whether submission passes G1, G2, or G3. To understand how consistent our pipeline is, and to choose default judge, we measure how often repeated judgments on the same submission agree. Consistency study setup. We compare two judges: GPT-6-Astra run within the Codex harness, and Claude-Opus5.5 run within the Claude Code harness. Both judges evaluate the same 52 submissions four times each under the same grading policy. We then measure the percentage of cases in which all four runs agree at three levels: the overall submission grade, each cumulative pass decision (G1, G1 G2, and G1 G2 G3), and the exact rating of each rubric node, treating unresolved and not-applicable ratings as distinct categories. We report 95% confidence intervals from 20,000 whole-paper bootstrap resamples. 16 Figure 7: User interface for editing the task specification and rubrics. We provide html page for scientists to edit, in which after the edits, they send back markdown file that contains those edits. Figure 8: Categorization of the edits made by scientists on the task specification and rubrics. We manually audit all 112 edits, group them into 12 categories for task specification edits and 8 categories for rubric edits. B.2 Experimental results The results are shown in Table 5. GPT-6-Astra produces more consistent paper-level decisions. GPT-6-Astra assigns the same overall grade across all four runs to 86.5% of submissions, compared with 57.7% for Claude-Opus-5.5. The gap holds for each cumulative pass decision, with 86.5% versus 69.2% on G1 and 100.0% versus 78.8% on G1 G2, while both judges are highly consistent on G1 G2 G3 (100.0% and 98.1%). Note that perfect agreement on the later decisions partly reflects that GPT-6-Astra rates no submission as passing G1 G2, so its verdicts there are uniformly negative. The decisions that vary across submissions, G1 and the overall grade, are therefore where the gap between the two judges is most informative. Node-level consistency does not translate into paper-level consistency. At the node level, Claude-Opus-5.5 is slightly more consistent than GPT-6-Astra on both the direction-specific rubric (94.9% versus 89.7%) and the integrity rubric (92.7% versus 87.6%), yet it is less consistent on every paper-level decision. Because each gate requires all of its nodes to pass, paper-level decision changes whenever single decisive node does. This suggests that the disagreements of Claude-Opus-5.5 more often fall on nodes that decide whether submission passes, while those of GPT-6-Astra more often fall on submissions that already fail on other nodes. Takeaway. Overall, GPT-6-Astra yields more reproducible paper-level decisions, which are what our main metric is computed from. We therefore use GPT-6-Astra as the default judge for all results in section 4, aggregating its four runs by majority vote. Note that consistency does not imply correctness, since judge can agree with itself while disagreeing with experts, which is why we also validate its judgments against expert criticisms in Table 4. Extended: Construction process Our construction and verification procedure for the task specifications and rubrics are as follows. Step 1: We have expert scientists propose follow-up direction in two or three sentences. one sentence version 17 of the directions are in Table 1. Alongside, we ask for specific constraints that must be taken into consideration to ensure that these are well represented in the subsequent steps. Step 2: We then use claude-code (Claude-Opus-5 max effort with claude-code-cli as the harness) to instantiate the follow-up direction into an initial version of the task specification and rubric. As explained in subsection 2.1, we require the task specification to be formatted in multiple sections, including the follow-up direction, components held fixed, design space, success conditions, required deliverables, conduct required, compute resources, and operating constraints. For the rubrics, we follow the json file rubric format from PaperBench [11]. Step 3: Since the task specfications and rubrics obtained from step 2 may not well represent the scientists intention of how the task should be formed or how the submissions should be graded, we further ask scientists to manually edit the content line-by-line. This includes adding new context (in the task specification) or nodes (in the direction-specific rubric and integrity check rubric), deleting them, and editing existing ones. This is done by sharing html file to scientists as shown in Figure 7 and asking them to send back the markdown files that contain these edits. Total of 112 edits were made on the task specification and rubrics and is illustrated in Figure 8. Below, for reference, we include all these 112 edits. Red marks wording removed or replaced in Before; blue marks wording added or substituted in After. Unchanged context remains unhighlighted. sections.title: Before
sections.content: A machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) maps an atomic environment {ri} to per-atom energy contribution Ei such that the total energy is E({ri}) = (cid:80) Ei and the forces = jE are analytic gradients. Most MLIPs in the spectral family SNAP, ACE, MTP separate this map into two stages: hand-engineered descriptor that maps an atoms neighborhood to fixed-length vector Bi RK , and regression model that maps Bi to Ei via fitted coefficients. The descriptor encodes three structural properties of the physics rotation, translation, and permutation invariance by construction. The regression model inherits those invariances for free.

sections.title: After
sections.content: A machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) maps an atomic environment {rij} to per-atom energy contribution Ei such that the total energy is E({ri}) = (cid:80) Ei and the forces = jE are analytic gradients with respect to neighboring atoms j. Most MLIPs in the density projection family SNAP, ACE, MTP separate this map into two stages: hand-engineered descriptor that maps an atoms neighborhood to fixed-length vector Bi RK , and regression model that maps Bi to Ei via fitted coefficients. The descriptor encodes three structural properties of the physics rotation, translation, and permutation invariance by construction. The regression model inherits those invariances for free. sections.content: 31 Moving from near-optimal to optimal is kernel-choice question: it is mathematical change to which ξ(k) is used in the LCHS integral, not change to how that integral is compiled into quantum circuit. sections.title: After
sections.content: Moving from near-optimal to optimal is kernel-choice question: it is mathematical change to which ξ(k) weight function is used in the LCHS integral, and change in how the weight function is computed via QSVT, but not change to how the integral itself is compiled into quantum circuit. The NovikauJoseph implementation framework (FCC-equivalent quadrature via the sinusoidal coordinate transformation + single QSP circuit + QSVT weight construction) is independent of the kernel and works for any kernel in the AnChildsLin family or any of the optimal extensions. Note, however, that the QSVT angles do need to be redetermined and reimplemented for any new choice of kernel weight function. Also, if the weight function is real, then this can be used to simplify the implementation of the kernel in the integral formula. The open question is which kernel, combined with this overall implementation structure, achieves the best end-to-end performance at the resolutions practical for digital emulation.
